qs.q: During a routine clinical handover, a surgical resident describes a patient's reported nausea and dizziness while documenting objective pallor and jaundice on physical examination. Which of the following features accurately distinguishes symptoms from signs?
o: Symptoms are patient‑reported experiences and are subjective.
Symptoms are objective findings identified by the examiner.
Signs are subjective experiences reported by the patient.
Signs are exclusively non‑measurable qualitative observations.
qs.e: Symptoms are defined as experiences reported by the patient and are usually subjective, whereas signs are objective findings identified during clinical examination. The source and nature of these findings define their category.

qs.q: An infant receiving total parenteral nutrition and broad-spectrum antibiotics for stage II necrotising enterocolitis develops direct hyperbilirubinaemia and conjugated jaundice. Which aspect of the ongoing management plan is the direct cause of bowel rest?
o: Maintain nil per os for seven to fourteen days
Place an orogastric tube with low intermittent suction
Perform serial abdominal examinations every four hours
qs.e: Bowel rest is achieved by stopping all enteral feeds (nil by mouth) for 7 to 14 days. Gastric decompression uses an orogastric or nasogastric tube, but the cessation of feeds is the defining feature of bowel rest.
qs.s: Necrotising Enterocolitis in the Newborn: MCQs

qs.q: A 62-year-old man presents with progressive painless jaundice, severe pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools for three weeks. On examination, he has a palpable, non-tender gallbladder and scratch marks. What is the most likely underlying mechanism for his palpable gallbladder?
o: Malignant obstruction of the common bile duct allowing normal distension
Primary cystic duct obstruction caused by a metastatic lymph node
A fibrosed, stone-containing gallbladder that cannot distend due to chronic inflammation
Acute cholecystitis secondary to pancreatic exocrine insufficiency
qs.e: According to Courvoisier's law, a palpable non-tender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient indicates a malignant obstruction of the common bile duct, as a stone-containing gallbladder is usually fibrosed and cannot distend. Gallstones typically cause painful jaundice and a contracted gallbladder rather than a palpable one.
qs.s: Pancreatic Head Cancer and Periampullary Tumours: Whipple Procedure: MCQs

qs.q: A 66-year-old man undergoes evaluation for obstructive jaundice. A contrast-enhanced pancreatic protocol CT scan reveals a pancreatic head mass with simultaneous dilation of both the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct. What is this classic finding called?
qs.e: The simultaneous dilation of the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct on imaging is known as the double duct sign, typical of pancreatic head cancer. Trousseau's sign refers to migratory thrombophlebitis associated with malignancy.
qs.s: Pancreatic Head Cancer and Periampullary Tumours: Whipple Procedure: MCQs

qs.q: A 65‑year‑old man with a pancreatic head tumor has a prolonged prothrombin time and INR due to obstructive jaundice. Which immediate intervention best corrects this coagulopathy before any invasive procedure?
o: Administer a single dose of vitamin K intravenously
Transfuse fresh‑frozen plasma to replace clotting factors
Place a biliary stent endoscopically to relieve obstruction
qs.e: Vitamin K deficiency from cholestasis prolongs PT/INR and is rapidly corrected by giving vitamin K. Fresh‑frozen plasma would only temporarily replace clotting factors without addressing the underlying deficiency.
qs.s: Pancreatic Head Cancer and Periampullary Tumours: Whipple Procedure: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following periampullary tumours typically presents with earlier jaundice and a higher resectability rate compared to pancreatic head adenocarcinoma?
o: Ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic body
Carcinoma of the ampulla of Vater
Neuroendocrine tumours of the islet cells
qs.e: Ampullary and duodenal tumours have a better prognosis because they present with earlier jaundice and higher resectability than pancreatic head cancer. Pancreatic body and tail tumours present much later and have a very low resectability rate.
qs.s: Pancreatic Head Cancer and Periampullary Tumours: Whipple Procedure: MCQs

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman is investigated for obstructive jaundice and weight loss. A tumour marker is checked which is elevated in over 70 to 80% of cases and is primarily used to monitor treatment response and recurrence rather than screening. Which marker is this?
qs.e: CA 19-9 is elevated in most pancreatic cancers and is used to monitor response and recurrence rather than screening due to false positives in benign biliary obstruction. Carcinoembryonic antigen is also raised but CA 19-9 is the primary marker for monitoring this malignancy.
qs.s: Pancreatic Head Cancer and Periampullary Tumours: Whipple Procedure: MCQs

qs.q: A 59-year-old man presents with progressive jaundice. A staging workup reveals a hard nodule felt on rectal examination in the rectovesical pouch. What is the traditional term for this late sign of unresectable intra-abdominal malignancy?
qs.e: Blumer's shelf refers to a palpable shelf in the rectovesical or rectouterine pouch indicating peritoneal seeding from advanced intra-abdominal cancer. Virchow's node is a left supraclavicular lymph node involvement.
qs.s: Pancreatic Head Cancer and Periampullary Tumours: Whipple Procedure: MCQs

es.q: Discuss the management of obstructive jaundice using PTC and PBD, including their indications, procedural techniques, drainage types, comparison with ERCP, and potential complications.
es.m:
- **Definition and Etiologies:** Obstructive jaundice results from interrupted bile flow into the duodenum, caused by choledocholithiasis, benign strictures, pancreatic head adenocarcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, or metastatic lymphadenopathy.
- **Role of ERCP vs PTC:** ERCP is generally the preferred first-line modality, but percutaneous transhepatic options are utilized when ERCP fails or is not technically feasible.
- **Indications:** Used for altered GI anatomy (Roux-en-Y, Billroth II), complex high hilar obstructions (Bismuth-Corlette III/IV), palliation of unresectable malignancies, and selective preoperative biliary decompression.
- **Contraindications:** Uncorrected coagulopathy (elevat
es.s: PTC and Percutaneous Biliary Drainage in Obstructive Jaundice: Essay questions

es.q: List and explain the two physiological phenomena responsible for neonatal physiologic jaundice.
es.m:
**Physiological Mechanisms:**
- Elevated bilirubin production due to increased breakdown of fetal erythrocytes.
- Low hepatic excretory capacity due to low concentrations of the binding protein ligandin in hepatocytes.
- Low activity of glucuronyl transferase, the enzyme responsible for binding bilirubin to glucuronic acid.
- Reduced conjugation leads to accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin, making it less water-soluble.

es.q: Outline the clinical progression of visible jaundice in a neonate and its diagnostic implication.
es.m:
**Clinical Progression:**
- Jaundice first becomes visible in the face and forehead.
- Identification is aided by pressure on the skin, as blanching reveals the underlying color.
- Jaundice gradually becomes visible on the trunk and extremities.
- Jaundice disappears in the opposite direction (from extremities to face).
- Visible jaundice in the lower extremities strongly suggests the need to check bilirubin levels.
- This visual assessment helps determine if serum or transcutaneous bilirubinometry is required.

es.q: List the specific indications for performing additional laboratory studies in an infant with jaundice.
es.m:
**Indications for Additional Labs:**
- Infants presenting with jaundice on the first day or after the third day of life.
- Infants who are anemic at birth.
- Infants who otherwise appear ill.
- Infants with serum bilirubin levels elevated enough to trigger treatment.
- Infants with significant jaundice persisting beyond the first 2 weeks of life.
- Infants with family, maternal, pregnancy, or case histories suggesting a pathologic process.
- Infants with physical examination findings not explained by simple physiologic hyperbilirubinemia.

ai.title: Neonatal and Infant Jaundice
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Jaundice is yellow discoloration of skin, sclerae and plasma caused by raised bilirubin. In low‑resource settings the clinician must rapidly differentiate haemolytic, physiological and obstructive causes and act to prevent kernicterus.

sections.p: Jaundice appears when total serum bilirubin (TSB) exceeds about 2 mg/dL (≈35 µmol/L). Diagnosis is clinical (yellow sclerae, skin) confirmed by a point‑of‑care bilirubinometer or laboratory TSB.
b: TSB ≥2 mg/dL in term infants, ≥3 mg/dL in preterm infants is visible jaundice
Direct (conjugated) fraction >20 % of TSB or >1 mg/dL suggests obstructive disease

sections.p: Severity is staged by TSB level and age in hours, using the Bhutani nomogram for term infants; preterm infants use the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) risk zones.
b: Low risk: TSB below 95th percentile for age
Intermediate risk: TSB 95‑99th percentile – consider phototherapy
High risk: TSB above 99th percentile – urgent phototherapy or exchange

sections.p: Causes are grouped by bilirubin metabolism site. In East African hospitals the most common are physiological, haemolytic (including G6PD deficiency), and sepsis‑related cholestasis.
b: Physiological: immature UDP‑glucuronosyltransferase, breast‑feeding jaundice
Haemolytic: G6PD deficiency, sickle cell disease, malaria‑induced hemolysis
Obstructive: biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, severe sepsis with cholestasis
Infectious: hepatitis B, HIV‑related cholestasis, malaria, typhoid

sections.p: The infant may be otherwise well or appear ill. Key clues are timing, stool/urine colour, and associated symptoms.
b: Onset <24 h → likely haemolysis
Onset 2‑7 days → physiological or breast‑feeding jaundice
Dark urine, pale stools → obstructive jaundice
Pruritus, acholic stools → cholestasis

sections.p: When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical clues: stool colour, timing, and hemolysis signs. Use bedside transcutaneous bilirubinometry if lab TSB cannot be obtained.

t.a: Total and direct bilirubin (point‑of‑care or lab)
t.b: Quantifies bilirubin and distinguishes conjugated vs unconjugated; direct >1 mg/dL indicates cholestasis
Detects allo‑immune hemolysis (ABO or Rh incompatibility)
Identifies enzymatic hemolysis common in East Africa

t.a: Complete blood count and reticulocyte count
t.b: Helps confirm hemolysis (high retics, low Hb)

t.a: Liver function panel (ALT, AST, ALP, GGT)
t.b: Elevated direct enzymes suggest cholestasis; transaminase rise points to hepatocellular injury
Looks for biliary dilatation, gallstones, or atresia

t.a: Urine dipstick for urobilinogen and bilirubin
t.b: Absent urobilinogen with dark urine supports obstructive jaundice

sections.p: Kernicterus is the most feared complication of severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
b: TSB >20 mg/dL in term or >15 mg/dL in preterm infants → risk of neurotoxicity
Lethargy, poor feeding, high‑pitch cry, seizures → early kernicterus
Persistent jaundice >2 weeks, pale stools, hepatomegaly → cholestatic disease

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then provide phototherapy and, if needed, exchange transfusion.
b: Physiological: Encourage feeding, monitor TSB, start phototherapy if >95th percentile
Haemolytic: Stop offending drugs, treat malaria or sickle crisis, give folic acid, consider exchange if TSB rapidly rises
Obstructive: Refer for surgical evaluation (e.g., Kasai for biliary atresia), start ursodeoxycholic acid if available
Phototherapy: Use blue‑light (460 nm) blankets; ensure eye protection
Exchange transfusion: Indicated when TSB exceeds exchange threshold or neurologic signs appear

sections.p: Regular TSB checks until levels fall below treatment thresholds; educate mothers on feeding and warning signs.
b: Re‑measure TSB 12‑hourly during phototherapy
Screen newborns for G6PD deficiency in high‑prevalence areas
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, treat maternal infections

sections.p: Conditions that cause yellow skin but have different pathophysiology.
b: Carotenemia – yellow skin from high carotene intake, sclerae remain white
Sepsis‑related mottling – does not produce scleral icterus

sections.p: Laboratory and bedside findings may be deceptive in low‑resource settings.
b: Transcutaneous bilirubin may underestimate TSB in dark‑skinned infants
Urine dipstick can give false‑negative bilirubin if urine is dilute

whenToSeekHelp: Lethargy, seizures, or poor feeding with jaundice
Dark urine and pale stools persisting >48 h

faq.a: Insufficient milk intake leads to dehydration and reduced bilirubin excretion.

faq.q: What is the significance of a direct bilirubin >1 mg/dL?
faq.a: It indicates cholestasis or hepatocellular injury rather than simple haemolysis.

faq.q: When is exchange transfusion preferred over phototherapy?
faq.a: When bilirubin exceeds the exchange threshold or the infant shows early neurologic signs.

exam: A term infant at 48 h has TSB 18 mg/dL, normal direct fraction, and is feeding poorly – what is the next step? — Initiate intensive phototherapy and monitor TSB every 6 h; consider exchange if rise >5 mg/dL in 12 h.

A 2‑week‑old presents with jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, and TSB 12 mg/dL (direct 8 mg/dL). What diagnosis is most likely and why? — Obstructive cholestasis (e.g., biliary atresia) because of predominant direct bilirubin and stool/urine changes.
How does G6PD deficiency alter your investigation plan in a jaundiced neonate? — Order a G6PD assay; avoid oxidant drugs; anticipate rapid bilirubin rise after hemolytic triggers.
Why is phototherapy less effective in infants with severe anemia? — Less hemoglobin reduces light absorption; also anemia may indicate ongoing hemolysis requiring additional treatment.

A child with malaria develops jaundice and a TSB of 15 mg/dL. What additional tests are essential? — Blood smear for parasitaemia, CBC, liver enzymes, and direct bilirubin to assess hemolysis vs cholestasis.
What red‑flag symptom distinguishes kernicterus from benign jaundice? — Neurologic changes such as lethargy, high‑pitch cry, or seizures.

In a low‑resource clinic without bilirubinometer, how would you decide on phototherapy? — Use visual assessment plus risk factors (age, prematurity, hemolysis) and treat if jaundice is obvious in a newborn <3 days old.
Why is ursodeoxycholic acid used in obstructive jaundice and not in haemolytic jaundice? — It improves bile flow in cholestasis; it has no effect on bilirubin production from hemolysis.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam differentiate physiological from pathological jaundice and identify red‑flags for haemolysis, cholestasis or sepsis in low‑resource settings.
b: Onset of visible jaundice (hours after birth, days, weeks).
Feeding pattern: exclusive breastfeeding, poor intake, weight loss.
Maternal risk factors: diabetes, G6PD deficiency, sickle cell trait, malaria exposure.
Family history of haemolytic disorders, liver disease or consanguinity.
Stool colour (yellow, acholic) and urine colour (dark, normal).
Any haemolysis signs: pallor, jaundiced sclera, hepatosplenomegaly, hemoglobinuria.
Systemic illness: fever, lethargy, poor perfusion, seizures.

t.b: Detects visible jaundice; distribution (head first) suggests unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; cannot quantify bilirubin level.
Looks for hepatomegaly (right upper quadrant fullness) and splenomegaly (left upper quadrant mass); positive suggests haemolysis or obstructive disease; cannot differentiate cause.
Liver edge >2 cm below costal margin indicates hepatomegaly; helps gauge severity of cholestasis; not specific for etiology.
Acholic stools point to conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; normal yellow stools favour unconjugated causes; bedside test cannot measure bile acid concentration.
Dark urine suggests conjugated bilirubin excretion; normal colour does not exclude haemolysis; bedside test cannot differentiate urobilinogen from bilirubin.

t.a: Capillary heel‑prick for rapid TSB (if bilirubinometer available)
t.b: Provides immediate bilirubin level to guide phototherapy; unavailable in many settings – rely on age‑specific visual chart.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a step‑wise approach: confirm total and direct bilirubin, assess haemolysis, evaluate liver function and rule out infection. When a test is unavailable, substitute clinical surrogates.
b: Total serum bilirubin (TSB) – answers overall bilirubin burden; compare to age‑specific nomogram (Bhutani) for phototherapy threshold.
Direct (conjugated) bilirubin – answers whether cholestasis is present; >2 mg/dL or >20 % of TSB warrants urgent imaging.
Complete blood count with reticulocyte count – answers presence of haemolysis; Hb <10 g/dL may affect phototherapy efficacy, retics >2 % support haemolysis.
Peripheral smear – answers red‑cell morphology; bite cells or Heinz bodies suggest G6PD deficiency.
Serum transaminases (ALT, AST) – answers hepatocellular injury; markedly raised (>5 × ULN) suggests viral hepatitis or sepsis.
Alkaline phosphatase and γ‑GT – answers cholestatic pattern; elevation >2 × ULN supports obstructive disease.
Blood group and Coombs test – answers immune haemolysis; positive direct Coombs indicates allo‑ or autoimmune haemolysis.
G6PD assay – answers enzyme deficiency; if unavailable, rely on smear and family history.
Hepatitis B surface antigen, HIV rapid test – answers infectious causes; positive results guide specific therapy.
Abdominal ultrasound – answers biliary anatomy; non‑visualised gallbladder or intra‑hepatic duct dilatation suggests biliary atresia.
If ultrasound unavailable, use serial stool colour charts and clinical progression to decide on referral.

t.b: If TSB above 95 th percentile → start phototherapy; above 99 th percentile → urgent phototherapy or exchange.

t.a: Direct bilirubin >2 mg/dL or >20 % of TSB
t.b: Triggers urgent abdominal imaging and referral for possible cholestasis.

t.a: Hb <10 g/dL with high retic count
t.b: Confirms haemolysis; consider G6PD testing; phototherapy still indicated but monitor for anemia.
Suggests hepatocellular injury; order viral hepatitis panel, consider sepsis work‑up.
Supports cholestatic process; proceed to imaging.
Indicates immune haemolysis; treat underlying cause, may need IVIG in severe cases.

t.a: Ultrasound finding of absent gallbladder or triangular cord sign
t.b: Highly suggestive of biliary atresia; refer for surgical evaluation within 60 days.
Use Kramer’s rule (skin colour by cephalocaudal progression) and age‑specific visual charts to estimate TSB.

sections.p: Classification integrates bilirubin kinetics, direct fraction and clinical context to guide treatment urgency.
b: Unconjugated jaundice: TSB ≥ 2 mg/dL (term) or ≥ 3 mg/dL (preterm) with direct ≤ 2 mg/dL and <20 % of total.
Conjugated jaundice: Direct > 2 mg/dL or > 20 % of TSB; mandates imaging within 24 h.
Bhutani risk zones for term infants: Low (<95 th), Intermediate (95‑99 th), High (>99 th).
Preterm phototherapy thresholds: use hour‑specific nomograms; generally lower than term.
Kernicterus risk: TSB > 20 mg/dL (term) or > 15 mg/dL (preterm) or rapid rise >0.5 mg/dL per hour.
Severe anaemia (Hb < 10 g/dL) may blunt phototherapy response; consider exchange if TSB continues to rise.
Cholestasis severity: Direct > 2 mg/dL plus alkaline phosphatase > 2 × ULN; urgent referral.

sections.p: Several disorders mimic neonatal jaundice; careful history, exam and targeted tests separate them.

t.b: Onset 2‑5 days, inadequate intake, TSB rises modestly (<15 mg/dL); stool normal; improve with feeding optimisation.
Onset >7 days, prolonged jaundice, TSB may exceed 15 mg/dL, stool normal; persists despite good intake; consider temporary cessation of breastfeeding.
Ill‑appearing infant, fever, direct bilirubin > 2 mg/dL, elevated CRP; requires blood cultures and broad‑spectrum antibiotics.
Rapid rise <24 h, dark urine, bite cells on smear, normal direct fraction; trigger avoidance of oxidative drugs.
Persistent conjugated jaundice >2 weeks, acholic stools, hepatomegaly, ultrasound absent gallbladder; early surgery improves outcome.
Severe unconjugated jaundice from birth, TSB > 20 mg/dL, no response to phototherapy; genetic confirmation; liver transplant definitive.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides care from immediate stabilization to definitive therapy, with clear triggers for escalation or referral in neonatal and pediatric jaundice.
b: 1. Ensure airway, breathing, circulation; treat hypoglycaemia and severe anaemia (Hb <10 g/dL) before phototherapy.
2. Confirm bilirubin type: if direct >2 mg/dL or >20 % of total, start urgent imaging (ultrasound) for obstructive causes.
3. Initiate phototherapy when TSB exceeds the 95th percentile for age on the Bhutani nomogram (or >2 mg/dL in term infants with risk factors).

4. Provide intensive feeding support (breast‑milk or formula) to promote bilirubin excretion; consider exchange transfusion if TSB >20 mg/dL in term or >15 mg/dL in preterm infants, or if neuro‑signs appear.

5. Treat underlying cause: antibiotics for sepsis, antimalarials for malaria‑induced haemolysis, folic acid for G6PD crisis, ursodeoxycholic acid for cholestasis, surgical referral for biliary atresia.
6. Monitor TSB every 4–6 h during phototherapy; stop when level falls below treatment threshold and remains stable for 12 h.
7. Escalate to exchange transfusion or specialist referral if TSB rises despite maximal phototherapy, if signs of kernicterus develop, or if imaging shows progressive obstruction.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key medications used in jaundice have predictable adverse profiles; awareness prevents iatrogenic harm.
b: Phototherapy: can cause dehydration, temperature loss, and skin rash; increase fluid intake and monitor temperature.
Ursodeoxycholic acid: may cause diarrhoea and mild hepatotoxicity; check liver enzymes weekly and adjust if ALT rises >3 × ULN.
Phenobarbital (rarely used to induce enzymes): can cause sedation and respiratory depression; avoid in infants with respiratory compromise.
Exchange transfusion fluids: risk electrolyte shifts; monitor serum potassium, calcium, and glucose during and after procedure.

t.b: Increase oral/IV fluids; weigh infant daily; check urine output >1 mL/kg/h.
Hold drug; repeat LFTs in 48 h; consider alternative cholestasis management.

sections.p: Recognize early signs of neuro‑toxicity, worsening cholestasis, or treatment failure to trigger higher‑level care.
b: Kernicterus: high‑pitched cry, lethargy, poor feeding, opisthotonus; immediate exchange transfusion and neuro‑imaging.
Acute bilirubin encephalopathy progression: seizures or flaccid tone; call neonatology urgently.
Persistent conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia >2 weeks with direct >2 mg/dL: arrange hepatobiliary scintigraphy or MRCP; refer to paediatric surgery.
Phototherapy failure: TSB rises >2 mg/dL above treatment threshold despite maximal irradiance; move to exchange transfusion.

sections.p: Co‑morbid conditions and local practices can mask or modify bilirubin dynamics, influencing both diagnosis and therapy.
b: HIV infection: may cause cholestasis from opportunistic infections or drug‑induced liver injury; check CD4, viral load, and review antiretrovirals.
Tuberculosis treatment (rifampicin): induces UDP‑glucuronosyltransferase, potentially lowering bilirubin; monitor for drug‑induced hepatitis.
Severe malnutrition: reduces albumin, altering bilirubin binding and increasing free bilirubin; supplement protein and monitor for re‑feeding syndrome.
Maternal diabetes: predisposes neonatal polycythaemia and haemolysis; obtain cord blood Hb and reticulocyte count.
Herbal remedies (e.g., traditional bitter herbs): may contain hepatotoxins; ask specifically and consider liver panel.
Renal failure: reduces bilirubin excretion via urine; adjust fluid balance and avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
Age extremes: preterm infants have immature conjugation; elderly patients may have reduced hepatic clearance and polypharmacy interactions.

sections.p: Tailor assessment and therapy to the physiological context of each population, especially where resources are limited.
b: Neonates (≤28 days): prioritize visual assessment, use transcutaneous bilirubinometer if available; phototherapy is first‑line; avoid exchange unless neuro‑signs.
Pregnant women with cholestasis: treat with ursodeoxycholic acid; monitor fetal well‑being; avoid phototherapy.
Elderly: look for obstructive causes (pancreatic cancer, gallstones); use ursodeoxycholic acid and consider ERCP; watch for drug‑induced cholestasis.
People with HIV: screen for opportunistic liver disease; adjust antiretroviral regimen if hepatotoxic; use ursodeoxycholic acid for cholestasis.

Low‑resource settings: use visual jaundice charts, bedside urine colour, stool colour cards; start phototherapy with locally built LED units; refer for imaging only when direct bilirubin >2 mg/dL or persistent >2 weeks.

facts: Visible jaundice in term infants usually appears when total serum bilirubin (TSB) ≥2 mg/dL (≈35 µmol/L).
In preterm infants visible jaundice appears at TSB ≥3 mg/dL.
Direct (conjugated) bilirubin >2 mg/dL or >20 % of total bilirubin indicates cholestasis and warrants urgent imaging.
Phototherapy is indicated when TSB exceeds the 95th percentile for age on the Bhutani nomogram (intermediate risk) or the 99th percentile (high risk).
Kernicterus risk rises sharply when TSB >20 mg/dL in term infants or >15 mg/dL in preterm infants.
Phototherapy efficacy falls in infants with hemoglobin <10 g/dL because of reduced skin oxygenation and altered bilirubin binding.
G6PD deficiency is the commonest haemolytic cause of neonatal jaundice in East Africa; trigger by fava beans, infections, or certain drugs.
Breast‑feeding jaundice peaks between days 3‑7 and improves with frequent feeding and adequate milk intake.

mnemonics.t: Age of onset, Bilirubin level, Conjugation (direct fraction), Duration – helps differentiate physiological, haemolytic, obstructive, and infection‑related causes.

vivas.q: Define kernicterus and list its earliest clinical signs.
vivas.a: Kernicterus is bilirubin‑induced neuronal injury; early signs are high‑pitch cry, lethargy, poor feeding, and hypotonia.

vivas.q: What bedside test helps distinguish unconjugated from conjugated jaundice when a bilirubinometer is unavailable?
vivas.a: Examine urine colour (dark urine suggests conjugated bilirubin) and stool colour (pale stools suggest cholestasis); also assess for scleral icterus.

vivas.q: Why is phototherapy less effective in infants with severe anemia?
vivas.a: Severe anemia (<10 g/dL) reduces skin blood flow and bilirubin transport to the dermis, lowering the amount of bilirubin available for photo‑isomerisation.

vivas.q: A term infant at 48 h has TSB 18 mg/dL, normal direct fraction, and is feeding poorly. What is the next step?
vivas.a: Start intensive phototherapy immediately and ensure adequate feeding or IV glucose to prevent further rise.

vivas.q: How does G6PD deficiency alter your investigation plan in a jaundiced neonate?
vivas.a: Add a peripheral smear for bite cells and Heinz bodies; avoid oxidative drugs; repeat bilirubin trend closely because haemolysis can be episodic.

vivas.q: Explain the significance of a direct bilirubin >2 mg/dL in a 2‑week‑old with dark urine and pale stools.
vivas.a: It indicates cholestasis; urgent abdominal ultrasound is required to look for biliary atresia or obstructive lesions.

vivas.q: When is exchange transfusion indicated in neonatal jaundice?
vivas.a: When TSB exceeds the exchange threshold on the Bhutani nomogram (usually >25 mg/dL in term infants) or if there are signs of acute kernicterus despite phototherapy.

vivas.q: What red‑flag symptom distinguishes kernicterus from benign jaundice?
vivas.a: Neurological signs such as high‑pitch cry, lethargy, or seizures.

vivas.q: In a low‑resource clinic without a bilirubinometer, how would you decide on phototherapy?
vivas.a: Use age‑specific visual assessment: if jaundice is visible in the sclera and skin of the trunk in a term infant >48 h, start phototherapy; confirm with serum bilirubin when possible.

vivas.q: Why is ursodeoxycholic acid used in obstructive jaundice but not in haemolytic jaundice?
vivas.a: It improves bile flow and reduces cholestasis; haemolytic jaundice is unconjugated and does not benefit from bile‑acid therapy.

vivas.q: List the two physiological phenomena responsible for neonatal physiologic jaundice.
vivas.a: Immature UDP‑glucuronosyltransferase activity and increased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin.

vivas.q: Outline the clinical progression of visible jaundice in a neonate and its diagnostic implication.
vivas.a: Day 1‑2: face; day 3‑5: trunk; day 6‑7: limbs – progression suggests physiological jaundice; early limb involvement (<24 h) suggests haemolysis.

vivas.q: When should additional laboratory studies (e.g., GGT, TORCH) be ordered in an infant with jaundice?
vivas.a: If direct bilirubin >2 mg/dL, jaundice persists >2 weeks, or there are associated signs such as hepatomegaly, pale stools, or failure to thrive.

vivas.q: A child with malaria develops jaundice and a TSB of 15 mg/dL. What additional tests are essential?
vivas.a: Check hemoglobin, peripheral smear for haemolysis, G6PD status, and liver function tests including ALT/AST and direct bilirubin.

vivas.q: What is the primary purpose of biliary drainage in obstructive jaundice?
vivas.a: To relieve cholestasis, reduce bilirubin levels, and prevent cholangitis while definitive treatment is planned.

vivas.q: Which laboratory profile confirms post‑hepatic cholestasis?
vivas.a: Elevated alkaline phosphatase and γ‑GT with direct bilirubin >2 mg/dL and a bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase ratio >0.5.

vivas.q: Why is ERCP often not feasible in a patient with Roux‑en‑Y gastric bypass presenting with obstructive jaundice?
vivas.a: The altered anatomy prevents endoscopic access to the papilla; a percutaneous or surgical approach is required.

vivas.q: What is the main contraindication for percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage in a coagulopathic patient?
vivas.a: An INR >1.5 or platelet count <50 × 10⁹/L due to high risk of bleeding.

vivas.q: What physiological phenomenon leads to the high bilirubin load in newborns with breast‑feeding jaundice?
vivas.a: Inadequate milk intake leads to reduced stool output, increasing enterohepatic recirculation of bilirubin.

mcqs.q: A 3‑day‑old term infant has TSB 12 mg/dL, direct fraction 0.4 mg/dL, and is feeding well. What is the most appropriate management?
mcqs.e: TSB is below the 95th percentile for age; observation and continued feeding are sufficient.

mcqs.q: A 2‑week‑old infant presents with jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, TSB 13 mg/dL, direct 9 mg/dL. Which investigation is most urgent?
mcqs.e: High direct bilirubin suggests cholestasis; ultrasound is needed urgently to assess biliary tract.

mcqs.q: In a neonate with G6PD deficiency, which drug should be avoided to prevent worsening haemolysis?
mcqs.e: Sulfonamides are oxidative and can precipitate haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical cause of neonatal physiological jaundice?
mcqs.e: ABO incompatibility causes pathological haemolysis, not physiological jaundice.

mcqs.q: A term infant at 48 h has TSB 19 mg/dL, hemoglobin 9 g/dL. What is the most likely effect on phototherapy?
mcqs.e: Hemoglobin <10 g/dL reduces skin blood flow, lowering phototherapy efficacy.

cases.v: A 5‑day‑old term male, exclusively breast‑fed, presents with yellowing of the face and trunk. TSB 14 mg/dL, direct 0.5 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12 g/dL. Mother reports feeding every 2 hours.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Physiological jaundice (breast‑feeding jaundice) due to inadequate intake.
Encourage more frequent feeding, monitor TSB, and start phototherapy if TSB rises above the 95th percentile.

qs.q: If TSB reaches 18 mg/dL at 72 h, what is the next step?
qs.a: Initiate intensive phototherapy; exchange transfusion is not indicated unless TSB exceeds the exchange threshold.

cases.v: A 3‑week‑old female, previously well, now has jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, hepatomegaly 4 cm below costal margin. TSB 11 mg/dL, direct 8 mg/dL, GGT 250 U/L.

qs.q: What is the most likely underlying condition?
qs.a: Obstructive cholestasis, most likely biliary atresia.

qs.q: Which investigation should be performed first?
qs.a: Abdominal ultrasound with assessment of gallbladder size and hepatic ducts.

qs.q: What definitive treatment is required if imaging confirms biliary atresia?
qs.a: Kasai portoenterostomy performed as early as possible, ideally before 8 weeks of age.

mistakes: Using a direct bilirubin cut‑off of 1 mg/dL alone to diagnose cholestasis – the correct threshold is >2 mg/dL or >20 % of total bilirubin.
Assuming phototherapy is ineffective in anaemia; the drop in efficacy occurs only when hemoglobin is <10 g/dL.
Ordering exchange transfusion based solely on an absolute TSB of 15 mg/dL without considering age‑specific nomogram percentiles.
Neglecting to assess stool colour; pale stools are a key bedside clue to conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
Confusing maternal diabetes as a cause of increased neonatal bilirubin via estrogen transfer – it predisposes to haemolysis, not higher bilirubin production.
Choosing percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage as first‑line for biliary atresia instead of early surgical Kasai portoenterostomy.
Failing to repeat bilirubin measurements after initiating phototherapy in a rapidly rising jaundice.
Prescribing phenobarbital for neonatal jaundice without confirming a pathological cause; it is not first‑line for physiological jaundice.
exam: Define kernicterus and list its earliest clinical signs. — Kernicterus is bilirubin‑induced neuronal injury; early signs are high‑pitch cry, lethargy, poor feeding, and hypotonia.

What bedside test helps distinguish unconjugated from conjugated jaundice when a bilirubinometer is unavailable? — Examine urine colour (dark urine suggests conjugated bilirubin) and stool colour (pale stools suggest cholestasis); also assess for scleral icterus.

Why is phototherapy less effective in infants with severe anemia? — Severe anemia (<10 g/dL) reduces skin blood flow and bilirubin transport to the dermis, lowering the amount of bilirubin available for photo‑isomerisation.

A term infant at 48 h has TSB 18 mg/dL, normal direct fraction, and is feeding poorly. What is the next step? — Start intensive phototherapy immediately and ensure adequate feeding or IV glucose to prevent further rise.

How does G6PD deficiency alter your investigation plan in a jaundiced neonate? — Add a peripheral smear for bite cells and Heinz bodies; avoid oxidative drugs; repeat bilirubin trend closely because haemolysis can be episodic.

Explain the significance of a direct bilirubin >2 mg/dL in a 2‑week‑old with dark urine and pale stools. — It indicates cholestasis; urgent abdominal ultrasound is required to look for biliary atresia or obstructive lesions.

When is exchange transfusion indicated in neonatal jaundice? — When TSB exceeds the exchange threshold on the Bhutani nomogram (usually >25 mg/dL in term infants) or if there are signs of acute kernicterus despite phototherapy.
